title: A river for a border, 1809
hookLine: a treaty with the British fixes the Sutlej as a boundary

cards: Riders on one bank, the young Maharaja's. On the other, the chiefs who live to the south, nervous, looking over their shoulders. Between them, a wide brown river carrying snowmelt down from the mountains: the Sutlej.
And behind them, a new power moving up from the east, the British East India Company, with its own army and its own plans. Two growing powers, one river between them.
Somebody has to decide where one ends and the other begins.

teach.b: First, the pressure. Ranjit Singh had been crossing the Sutlej, drawing the chiefs south of it into his orbit.
Some of them, including the Phulkian houses this path met earlier, turned to the British for protection, and the Company sent an envoy, Charles Metcalfe, to the Maharaja's camp. Second, the bargain.
The talks were tense, and the histories say they nearly broke more than once.
In the end, at Amritsar, the two sides signed a treaty. The Sutlej would be the line. South of it, the British would protect the chiefs.
North of it, the Maharaja was free to build his kingdom, and the Company would leave him alone. Third, what it cost and what it gave.
It cost him a dream of ruling all the Sikh lands on both banks, a real loss. But it gave him peace on his eastern side, and he turned his energy north and west instead.
The histories say he kept his word: as long as he lived, he did not cross that line in force.
In Japji, Guru Nanak says the bull that holds the earth in place is dharma, born of compassion, and that contentment is the thread holding it steady. Santokh, contentment, is a Sikh virtue.
Not giving up: knowing where your line is, and letting that knowledge hold your world steady. A powerful man, drawing a line he could have pushed.

how: Sikh histories remember the treaty of Amritsar, which made the Sutlej the line between Ranjit Singh's kingdom and the British, and santokh, contentment, is named among the virtues in Sikh teaching.

games.q: you're the Maharaja. the British will guard the chiefs south of the Sutlej. you could fight for both banks, or accept the river as your line. what do you do?
o: accept the river line, and turn north and west.
fight the Company for both banks.
games.why: he signed the treaty at Amritsar and kept to it. it cost him his hopes south of the river, and gave him peace on that side.

practice: Think of one boundary in your life that matters, a friend's privacy, a coworker's time, a promise to yourself, a no you'd like to push on, and let it be a river, quiet and clear.
You could cross it, and you choose not to; notice whether that feels like relief, or ache, or both, and if you pray, let Waheguru come with each breath out.
